title: CHAPTER THREE. On the immortality of the soul from the confession of the best philosophers and from reasons
english: CHAPTER THREE. On the immortality of the soul from the confession of the best philosophers and from reasons.
Hitherto the immortality of the soul has been established from the confession of the Gentile barbarians: now the same will be demonstrated from the consensus and reasons of the best philosophers.

title: I. Not the best: Epicurus, Lucretius, Dicaearchus, Panaetius, and the Stoics deny or dilute immortality
english: I. I say of the best philosophers, because there are not lacking philosophers of no best sense who have denied, attacked, or at least called into doubt the immortality of the soul. Epicurus, parting company with the better ones, embraced a sentence worthy of himself; Lucretius following him in the third book which he wrote On the Nature of Things attacks the immortality of the soul with good and elegant verses indeed, but with bad and weaker arguments, and tries to prove that minds and light souls are native to living things and mortal. Nay more, as Cicero witnesses in Tusculan Disputations book 1, troops of contradictors come — not only of Epicureans, but Dicaearchus also discoursed against this immortality and wrote three books in which he tries to make souls mortal. So also Panaetius wants them to perish. But the Stoics grant us a loan as to crows: they say minds will remain long, they deny forever.

title: Stoics on the soul's duration; Cleanthes and Chrysippus; Pliny impiously mocks immortality
english: The same Stoics, according to Diogenes Laertius book 6 on Zeno, [hold the soul] to be generated twice.at all remain until the conflagration; but Chrysippus only those of the wise. Pliny, a philosopher not of better mark, in Natural History book 7, chapter 33, impiously mocks the sentence on the immortality of souls: Those, he says, are inventions of childish deliriums and of a greed never to cease from mortality.

title: Peripatetic interpreters Alexander and Averroes; Pomponazzi; Galen vs Plato; Isidore of Pelusium
english: Next from the Peripatos there are two interpreters of Aristotle, one Greek — Alexander of Aphrodisias — the other Arab, namely Averroes: both place outside man the agent intellect, which alone they admit to be immortal; to which opinion of Averroes in the previous century Peter Pomponazzi alluded in disputing, and thereby provoked the censure of Pope Leo X in the Lateran Council, session 8. Galen also either denied the immortality of the soul or called it into doubt. For although somewhere he speaks so that he might seem less alien from admitting it, yet in the book That manners follow the temperament of the body he rebukes Plato for asserting the immortality of the mind.

Oppose to him what Isidore of Pelusium, the excellent disciple of the great Chrysostom, says against him in book 4, letter 125. Concerning the cure of bodies, he says, since that man is a most excellent craftsman in this art, let him speak by his own judgment: but concerning the soul let him not take up a contest with the wise nor descend into a struggle for which he is neither trained nor prepared. Galen was indeed a most excellent man in philosophy and medicine, and an impious mocker of the doctrine of Moses, who even in On the Use of Parts book 10 dared to deny that God, if he wished, could make a horse or an ox from ashes — much more, as it seems, about to deny that the first man was produced from a clod of earth, or that the body of each man already reduced to dust would be raised again the same in number.

title: II. Paradox: some who acknowledge Scripture deny immortality — Sadducees; Arabians; John XXIII
english: II. But a wonder has occurred: that what by nature's instinct among barbarian nations, and by best reason among the learned (if you except a few), was received without Scripture, that very thing has been denied by some who have acknowledged Scripture. The Sadducees of old taught that there is no resurrection, nor angel, nor spirit (that is, immortal) (Acts 23:8). See also Josephus, Antiquities book 18, chapter 2, and Jewish War book 2, chapter 7. Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History book 6, chapter 30, reports that certain persons arose in Arabia in the third century who so denied the immortality of souls that they did not meanwhile abolish the resurrection, but affirmed that the soul is also raised again together with the body. Augustine from Eusebius mentions the same in Heresies 83. Then John XXIII, Roman Pontiff, said and stubbornly believed that the soul is extinguished and dies together with the human body, otherwise of brutes, as the words of the Council of Constance, session 11, have it.

title: Photinians imply mortality; Tertullian assigns body yet vindicates immortality
english: The Photinians of this age lay down those principles from which the mortality of the soul must necessarily be concluded, in the Racovian Catechism, in order to attack the union of the divine and human natures in Christ, in the chapter on the knowledge of Christ. So they say that two substances adverse in properties cannot come together into one person, as mortal and immortal are. Tertullian ascribes a corporeal nature, yet does not take away immortality, but rather vindicates it sharply. But he seems to call every created thing that truly subsists a body, as also Hilary in his Matthew canon 5; therefore he ought not to be numbered among those errors: yet what he ascribes in On the Soul chapter 9 — length, breadth, and height, by which philosophers measure bodies — cannot be excused or explained by any convenient reason. And chapter 36: The soul, he says, sown in the womb together with the flesh, together with it also obtains sex. These things are to be trembled at, not laughed at, as Augustine witnesses in On Genesis Literally book 20, the last chapters.

title: III. Best philosophers asserting immortality: Pherecydes, Pythagoras, metempsychosis; Druids, Brahmans, Pharisees
english: III. The best philosophers asserting the immortality of the soul are Greeks or Latins. Pherecydes the Syrian, as Cicero witnesses in Tusculan Disputations book 1, was first or among the first, and his disciple was Pythagoras, who, though he knew the soul to be immortal, yet did not have it known what happens to it after departure from the body, and embraced metempsychosis, concerning which Ovid in Metamorphoses book 15 introduces him speaking thus: Souls lack death, and always, the former seat left behind, they live in new homes and dwell in those received. The Druids of the Gauls, embracing Pythagoras's opinion, according to Julius Caesar, Gallic War book 6, wish above all to persuade this — that souls do not perish, but after death pass from some to others. And the Brahmans who still survive among the Indians today profess themselves disciples of Pythagoras, as Linschoten witnesses, part 1, chapter 38, and believe that souls are immortal, yet so that they transmigrate from one body into another, and that there is no difference whether they fly into a brute or a human body, according as each has done well or ill. This reciprocal recurring discourse of souls, as Tertullian calls it in On the Soul chapter 28, the Pharisees also of old believed, as Josephus witnesses in Jewish War book 2, chapter 7, and Antiquities book 18, chapter 2; concerning Herod the tetrarch and the Jews the same seems to be gathered from Matthew 14:2 and 16:14 and Luke 9:7.

title: III continued. Among the Greeks Plato and Aristotle held soul-immortality certain and clear
english: Among the Greeks, among the chiefs of philosophers, for Socratic Plato and for Aristotle the immortality of the soul was a certain and clear thing. For even Cicero, however devoted to the Stoics, thinks those who dissent from Plato and Socrates and from that family ought to be called plebeian philosophers (Tusculan Disputations book 1). Plato pursues this matter expressly in the Phaedo, which when read Cleombrotus of Ambracia, as the same Cicero reports from Callimachus's epigram, though nothing adverse had befallen him, threw himself from a wall into the sea — whom Jerome in letter 25 calls a martyr of foolish philosophy. See also, if you please, Plato in the Phaedrus, Timaeus, Philebus, and Republic; and among Platonists above the rest Marsilio Ficino in Platonic Theology, or On the Immortality of the Soul, a far most learned treatise.

Aristotle left contexts not to be despised for the immortality of the soul in the books On the Soul: book 1, contexts 65 and 66 — he says the intellect does not perish, is something divine and impassible; book 2, context 21 — that the intellect is a diverse genus of the soul, and this alone is separated, as eternal from corruptible; book 3, contexts 4, 6, 7, and 19 — he teaches that it, since it understands universals, is neither mixed nor corporeal; likewise separable from the body, though sense cannot be separated. And context 20 he expressly says immortal and eternal. And On the Generation of Animals book 2, chapter 3: It remains that the intellect alone enters from outside and alone is divine. For it has nothing in common by its act with bodily act.

title: IV. Among the Latins Cicero and Seneca vote for soul-immortality; Tertullian on what nature knows
english: IV. Among the Latins Cicero and Seneca stand for all, who vote for the immortality of the soul. Cicero in On Friendship under the person of Laelius does not assent to those who have begun to argue that souls perish together with bodies, and that all things are destroyed by death. And in Tusculan Disputations book 1 he brings reasons into the middle, as also in On Old Age. But Seneca so often inculcates the immortality of the soul that he seems to have been wholly in it. See Consolation to Marcia chapter 24; to Helvia his mother chapter 11; letters 85 and 102. From which testimonies it is gathered how wisely and rightly Tertullian pronounced in On the Resurrection chapter 3: certain things are known from nature, as the immortality of the soul among many, as our God among all.

title: V. Heap of reasons after authorities; Ficino and Petrus Gregorius; RATIO I from operations of intellect
english: V. Thus far have been the authorities of the best philosophers: to these can be added not a few reasons by which they were accustomed to establish the immortality of the soul. A heap of reasons after Plato, Aristotle, and Cicero for the immortality of the soul, and a refutation of contrary sophisms, are exhibited especially by Marsilio Ficino in his Platonic Theology, and by Petrus Gregorius of Toulouse in the volume of his Commentary on the Wonderful Art concerning the immortality of the soul. For us these suffice which are sought from its operations and rest, and from the chief inconveniences of the contrary opinion.

REASON I is from the operations of the intellect. For whoever conceives and knows the genera of all things, all grades of natures, even spiritual things such as God and intelligences, and is not, like bodily senses, hurt and weakened by perceiving such excellent objects, but rather is perfected, is reflected upon himself, and understands what and how he knows, abstracts universals from singulars, and those immaterial things have a reason of futures, compares these, and gathers what is of use: he is immortal. But the rational soul by its intellect produces operations of such a kind. Therefore it is immortal.

title: REASON II from operations of will; REASON III from the soul's ultimate rest
english: II. From the operations of the will. That which by its will is so carried toward every good as the intellect toward every true thing, delights in the beauty of all things, and in admiring the artifice that shines in singulars, and also in just and honest actions and liberal disciplines; is free, and can itself specify its actions and determine to either part of opposites; often also resists its own body, rules its affections, and operates contrary to what they urge: that is immortal. But the rational soul by its will produces such operations. Therefore it is immortal.

III. From its ultimate rest. Whatever nothing non-eternal fills, and for which neither time nor place nor life nor pleasure nor honor nor empire nor finally any good, however great, when apprehended as mortal and something about to fail, neither all these together nor each singly so satisfy that it rests in them: that is eternal and immortal. But the rational soul is such. Therefore it is immortal and eternal.

title: REASON IV from inconveniences of the contrary; Wisdom 2; VI use of these reasons — Cap. 3 close
english: IV. From the chief inconveniences of the contrary opinion. For if the sentence on the immortality of souls is taken away from human minds, and the contrary persuasion of their destruction is put in its place, there is also taken away and overturned not only all worship of deity and religion, but whatever there is among men of integrity, virtue, justice, and honesty; and from the opposite side is introduced and confirmed the pursuit of the body's delights and pleasures, and a life wholly given to filling carnal desires, and placing the highest good in such enjoyments and delights. For if the soul is of the same nature and condition with flesh or body, why should it pursue anything other than what is pleasing to flesh and body? And if nothing of man remains after the destruction of the flesh, and he lasts only so long as his flesh, why should he not have care of his flesh alone, that by its benefit he may survive as long as possible? Why should he ever discomfort or oppose his flesh? Why look to anything but what is present, and by which the body may be well and kept stuffed and covered?

That these inconveniences necessarily follow the denied immortality of souls has been observed in Wisdom 2, where at verse 1 the wicked first deny and mock it; then, this hypothesis made, they plunge themselves wholly into pleasures (verses 6 and following); third the wise man adds how, that they may have whence to care for their skin and live genially, they spoil and afflict others, and serving their affections define by their power what is lawful and honest (verses 10, 11 and following); fourth the wise man concludes at verse 21 that these have erred in judgment.
VI. THE USE of these reasons is: 1. that we presuppose them in our theology; 2. that we have them ready, so that when need arises we may turn them against those who do not receive the Scriptures.
